blocks.html: Most Indian health statistics, from the SRS infant mortality rate to a district’s crude death rate, are rates or ratios, and comparing them across places is fair only after adjusting for age structure. This section defines the building blocks and the core indicators (§7.4.1), shows the two ways of removing the effect of age, direct (§7.4.2) and indirect (§7.4.3), and attaches confidence intervals to rates, rate ratios and SMRs (§7.4.4). It builds on the one-line definitions of prevalence, risk and rate (recall §1.5) and uses the weighted mean (recall §2.2.2), the Poisson distribution (recall §5.7.1.3) and the CIs of §7.2.
Ratios, Proportions, Rates and Health Indicators

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
• A ratio is one quantity divided by another; the numerator need not be part of the denominator (e.g. doctors per 10,000 population).
  • A proportion is a ratio whose numerator is part of its denominator (CDC, 2012a).
  • A rate is the frequency of an event in a defined population over a specified period (CDC, 2012a). Its denominator is person-time: the total time at risk, summed across people. For a whole population over one year, person-time is estimated by the mid-year population × 1 year (CDC, 2012b).
  • Crude rates use the whole population. Specific rates restrict numerator and denominator to one age group, sex or cause. Proportional (proportionate) mortality is deaths from one cause divided by all deaths, a proportion, not a rate (CDC, 2012b).
  • Incidence counts new cases in a period; prevalence counts all existing cases at a point or during a period (CDC, 2012c).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
A count means little until you know how many people, over how long, produced it. A rate adds the person-time, so districts of different sizes can be compared. The indicators you meet in SRS reports and NFHS fact sheets are all numerator/denominator pairs, and many exam questions on them turn on getting the denominator right: live births, total births or the mid-year population.

Prevalence, incidence and duration. Prevalence depends on both incidence and the duration of illness (CDC, 2012c). A simple steady-state argument shows how.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
In a stable population of size N with C current cases, new cases arise at rate I among the N − C people without the disease, and cases end (by cure or death) after an average duration D, so about C/D end each year. If prevalence is steady, inflow equals outflow:

I × (N − C) = C/D ⇒ C/(N − C) = I × D.

C/(N − C) is P/(1 − P), where P = C/N. When P is small, 1 − P ≈ 1, so P ≈ I × D. Example: incidence 2 per 1,000 per year and mean duration 5 years give P ≈ 0.002 × 5 = 1% (the exact steady-state value is 0.99%).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
The core indicators, with the definitions used by WHO and CDC:

Indicator Numerator Denominator Per
Crude birth rate (CBR) Live births in the year Mid-year population 1,000
Crude death rate (CDR) Deaths in the year Mid-year population 1,000
Infant mortality rate (IMR) Deaths under 1 year of age Live births in the same year 1,000 live births
Neonatal mortality rate (NMR) Deaths in the first 28 completed days Live births 1,000 live births
Perinatal mortality rate (PMR) Stillbirths (≥ 28 weeks) + early neonatal deaths (days 0–6) Total births (live births + stillbirths) 1,000 births
Maternal mortality ratio (MMR) Maternal deaths (pregnancy or within 42 days of its end, from related causes) Live births 100,000 live births
Total fertility rate (TFR) Sum of age-specific fertility rates, 15–49 (× 5 for 5-year groups) (children per woman) —
Case fatality rate (CFR) Deaths from the disease among cases Cases of the disease 100

Sources: WHO Indicator Metadata Registry for IMR, NMR, PMR, MMR and TFR; CDC (2012b, 2012d) for CBR, CDR and CFR; the SRS enumerator manual defines a stillbirth as a fetal death at 28 or more weeks of gestation (quoted in Dandona et al., 2023).

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
A hypothetical vital-events register for District A (mid-year population 100,000; the population and deaths are those of District A in §7.4.2, the two-district standardisation example):

  1. Live births 2,000 → CBR = 2,000/100,000 × 1,000 = 20 per 1,000.
  2. Deaths 789 → CDR = 789/100,000 × 1,000 = 7.89 per 1,000.
  3. Infant deaths 60 → IMR = 60/2,000 × 1,000 = 30 per 1,000 live births. Of these, 40 were neonatal deaths → NMR = 20, and post-neonatal mortality = (60 − 40)/2,000 × 1,000 = 10.
  4. Stillbirths 30 and early neonatal deaths 28 → PMR = (30 + 28)/(2,000 + 30) × 1,000 = 28.6 per 1,000 births. Note the denominator includes stillbirths.
  5. Maternal deaths 2 → MMR = 2/2,000 × 100,000 = 100 per 100,000 live births.
  6. Age-specific fertility rates per 1,000 women aged 15–19, 20–24, … 45–49: 15, 140, 120, 65, 25, 8, 2. TFR = 5 × (15 + 140 + 120 + 65 + 25 + 8 + 2)/1,000 = 5 × 0.375 = 1.9 children per woman (1.875).
  7. A dengue outbreak: 250 cases, 4 deaths among them → CFR = 4/250 × 100 = 1.6%.

points.html: IMR is not a true rate. Its denominator is live births, not person-time, and WHO defines it as a life-table probability of dying before age 1, expressed per 1,000 live births (WHO IMR metadata; §7.5 shows this probability).

MMR ratio vs rate. The maternal mortality ratio divides by live births (a proxy for pregnancies) (WHO MMR metadata). A maternal mortality rate divides by women of reproductive age. Check which one a report uses.

CFR is a proportion. WHO notes that “case fatality rate” is strictly a misnomer because there is no time component, and uses “case fatality ratio” instead (WHO, 2020). It measures severity, not risk to the population. During an ongoing outbreak it is biased by unresolved cases.
Denominators to memorise: births (IMR, NMR, MMR); total births including stillbirths (PMR, stillbirth rate); mid-year population (CBR, CDR, specific rates).
Data sources (recall §1.4.4): SRS gives state-level vital rates; NFHS gives survey-based estimates with CIs. Stillbirths appear under-reported in SRS relative to NFHS (Dandona et al., 2023).

blocks.label: Checkpoint 7.5

questions.prompt: A block with a mid-year population of 60,000 registers 1,500 live births, 42 infant deaths (27 of them neonatal), 25 stillbirths, 18 early neonatal deaths and 3 maternal deaths. Compute the CBR, IMR, NMR, PMR and MMR.
questions.answer:
• CBR = 1,500/60,000 × 1,000 = 25 per 1,000 population.
  • IMR = 42/1,500 × 1,000 = 28 per 1,000 live births.
  • NMR = 27/1,500 × 1,000 = 18 per 1,000 live births.
  • PMR = (25 + 18)/(1,500 + 25) × 1,000 = 43/1,525 × 1,000 = 28.2 per 1,000 births (the denominator includes stillbirths).
  • MMR = 3/1,500 × 100,000 = 200 per 100,000 live births.

questions.prompt: Why is the case fatality rate not a rate, and why can it mislead early in an outbreak?
questions.answer: It is a proportion (deaths among cases ÷ cases) with no time component, so it measures severity, not a rate of occurrence. Early in an outbreak, detected cases are skewed towards severe ones (inflating it), and some current cases have not yet died or recovered (deflating it).

questions.prompt: Diabetes has a prevalence of 10% in a town, and people live with it for an average of 20 years. Assuming a steady state, what is the approximate annual incidence among people without diabetes?
questions.answer: P/(1 − P) = I × D, so 0.10/0.90 = 0.111 = I × 20, giving I = 0.0056 per year, about 5.6 new cases per 1,000 people without diabetes per year. The shortcut P ≈ I × D gives 0.10/20 = 5 per 1,000; it underestimates here because a prevalence of 10% is not small.

blocks.html: Direct Standardisation

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
A directly age-standardised rate (DSR) is the death rate a study population would have if it had the age structure of a chosen standard population. It is a weighted mean of the study population’s age-specific rates, weighted by the standard population’s age distribution (recall §2.2.2):

DSR = Σ(rᵢ × Sᵢ)/ΣSᵢ,

where rᵢ is the study population’s rate in age group i and Sᵢ the standard population in that group.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Death rates rise steeply with age, so an older district can have a higher crude death rate even if every age group in it is healthier. A crude rate is itself a weighted mean of age-specific rates, with the district’s own age structure as weights. Direct standardisation swaps in the same weights for both districts, so any remaining difference reflects the age-specific rates, not the age mix (CDC, 2012b).

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
Two districts of 100,000 people each (data/standardisation_districts.csv); standard population 100,000.

Steps 1–2: the two districts.

Age Pop A Deaths A Rate A /1000 Pop B Deaths B Rate B /1000
0–4 9,000 90 10.0 16,000 208 13.0
5–14 17,000 17 1.0 26,000 39 1.5
15–29 26,000 39 1.5 28,000 56 2.0
30–44 22,000 55 2.5 16,000 51 3.19
45–59 16,000 128 8.0 9,000 90 10.0
60+ 10,000 460 46.0 5,000 280 56.0
Total 100,000 789 7.89 (crude) 100,000 724 7.24 (crude)

Steps 3–4: expected deaths in the standard population.

Age Standard pop Expected at A’s rates Expected at B’s rates
0–4 10,000 100.0 130.0
5–14 20,000 20.0 30.0
15–29 27,000 40.5 54.0
30–44 20,000 50.0 63.75
45–59 14,000 112.0 140.0
60+ 9,000 414.0 504.0
Total 100,000 736.5 921.75
  1. Crude rates: A = 789/100,000 × 1,000 = 7.89; B = 7.24 per 1,000. A looks worse (crude rate ratio 1.09).
  2. Age-specific rates: B is higher in every age group.
  3. Expected deaths in the standard population, at each district’s own rates: multiply each rate by the standard population and divide by 1,000 (e.g. 0–4 in A: 10.0 × 10,000/1,000 = 100).
  4. DSR_A = 736.5/100,000 × 1,000 = 7.36 per 1,000; DSR_B = 921.75/100,000 × 1,000 = 9.22 per 1,000.
  5. Standardised rate ratio A/B = 7.36/9.22 = 0.80. After age adjustment, A’s mortality is 20% lower than B’s; the crude ranking was reversed.
  6. Why: 10% of A’s people are 60 or older against 5% of B’s, and deaths at 60+ make up 58% of A’s deaths but only 39% of B’s (Figure 7.3).

blocks.alt: Age structure and age-specific death rates in two districts
blocks.caption: Figure 7.3. Left: District A has twice B’s share of people aged 60+. Right: B’s age-specific death rates are higher in every age group (log scale). The crude rates favour B; the directly standardised rates favour A.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
library(epitools)
sd <- read.csv("data/standardisation_districts.csv")
round(1000 * ageadjust.direct(count = sd$deathsA, pop = sd$popA,
                              stdpop = sd$std_pop), 2)
round(1000 * ageadjust.direct(count = sd$deathsB, pop = sd$popB,
                              stdpop = sd$std_pop), 2)
crude.rate   adj.rate        lci        uci 
      7.89       7.36       6.86       7.90 
crude.rate   adj.rate        lci        uci 
      7.24       9.22       8.51       9.97

crude.rate and adj.rate are steps 1 and 4 (multiplied by 1,000 to read per 1,000). lci and uci are 95% confidence limits for each DSR (§7.4.4). The two intervals do not overlap, so the reversal is not a small-number artefact.

points.html: The DSR is a comparison device. Its value depends on the standard chosen. Only DSRs computed with the same standard can be compared.

Requirements. Direct standardisation needs the age-specific rates of each study population. With few deaths per age group those rates are unstable; indirect standardisation (§7.4.3) is then preferred.

Confounding by age. The crude-versus-standardised reversal is an example of confounding (§11.6: a third variable, here age, linked to both the “exposure”, district, and the outcome, death). Standardisation is one way to control it.

blocks.html: Indirect Standardisation and the SMR

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
Indirect standardisation applies a standard population’s age-specific rates to the study population’s own age structure, giving the expected deaths (E). The standardised mortality ratio is

SMR = observed deaths (O)/expected deaths (E).

SMR = 1 means mortality as expected from the standard rates; SMR = 1.23 means 23% more deaths than expected.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Indirect standardisation asks: “If this district died at the standard rates, how many deaths would we expect, given its own age mix?” It needs only the district’s total deaths and its population by age, not its age-specific death rates, so it works when those rates are unreliable or unknown, for example in a small PHC catchment or an occupational cohort.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html: E = Σ(Rᵢ × nᵢ), where Rᵢ is the standard rate and nᵢ the study population in age group i. O = Σ(rᵢ × nᵢ). So SMR = Σ(rᵢnᵢ)/Σ(Rᵢnᵢ): the study population’s own rates relative to the standard rates, both weighted by the study population’s age structure. Multiplying the standard population’s crude rate by the SMR gives an indirectly standardised rate.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
Standard rates per 1,000 (last column of data/standardisation_districts.csv): 9.0, 1.2, 1.8, 2.9, 8.5, 48.0.

  1. E_A = (9.0 × 9,000 + 1.2 × 17,000 + 1.8 × 26,000 + 2.9 × 22,000 + 8.5 × 16,000 + 48.0 × 10,000)/1,000 = 81 + 20.4 + 46.8 + 63.8 + 136 + 480 = 828.0.
  2. SMR_A = 789/828.0 = 0.95: A has 5% fewer deaths than expected.
  3. E_B = 144 + 31.2 + 50.4 + 46.4 + 76.5 + 240 = 588.5.
  4. SMR_B = 724/588.5 = 1.23: B has 23% more deaths than expected.
  5. Indirectly standardised rates: the standard population’s crude rate is 7.72 per 1,000, so ISR_A = 7.72 × 0.953 = 7.35 and ISR_B = 7.72 × 1.230 = 9.49 per 1,000. Direct and indirect methods agree that B has the higher mortality.

points.html: Direct vs indirect. Direct: needs study age-specific rates, uses standard population weights, gives a DSR. Indirect: needs study age structure and total deaths, uses standard rates, gives an SMR.

Each SMR compares one population with the standard. The derivation shows that each SMR weights by its own population’s age structure, so two SMRs are averages over different weights. Comparing them is fair only if the ratio rᵢ/Rᵢ is similar across age groups. Here it ranges from 0.83 to 1.11 in A and from 1.10 to 1.44 in B, so the DSRs of §7.4.2 are the better basis for ranking A against B.
The same logic gives standardised incidence ratios (SIR) for cancer registries and standardised ratios for hospital mortality.

blocks.html: Confidence Intervals for Rates, Rate Ratios and SMRs

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
When a count d of events arises from independent events in a large population, d follows a Poisson distribution (recall §5.7.1.3) with variance equal to its mean, so SE(d) ≈ √d. Hence:

  • Rate r = d/PT (PT = person-time): SE(r) = √d/PT, and 95% CI = r ± 1.96√d/PT (or the exact Poisson interval when d is small).
  • Rate ratio RR = r₁/r₂: SE(ln RR) = √(1/d₁ + 1/d₂), and 95% CI = RR × exp(± 1.96 × SE).
  • SMR = O/E: exact Poisson limits for O divided by E, or approximately SMR × exp(± 1.96/√O).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The precision of a rate depends on the number of events, not on the size of the population. 789 deaths among 100,000 people give the same relative precision as 789 deaths among 10 million. Ratios are handled on the log scale, where their sampling distribution is closer to Normal and the interval comes back asymmetric.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
SE of a log count. For a Poisson count, Var(d) = d. A small change in d changes ln d by about (1/d) × the change, so Var(ln d) ≈ (1/d)² × Var(d) = (1/d)² × d = 1/d.

SE of a log rate ratio. ln RR = ln d₁ − ln d₂ − ln PT₁ + ln PT₂. The person-times are fixed, and d₁ and d₂ are independent, so variances add (as in §7.2.3): Var(ln RR) = 1/d₁ + 1/d₂.

SMR. E is computed from standard rates and treated as fixed, so all the uncertainty is in O: Var(ln SMR) ≈ 1/O.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Crude death rate of District A. d = 789, PT = 100,000 person-years. SE = √789/100,000 = 0.00028 = 0.28 per 1,000. 95% CI = 7.89 ± 1.96 × 0.28 = 7.34 to 8.44 per 1,000.
  2. Crude rate ratio A/B. RR = 7.89/7.24 = 1.09. SE(ln RR) = √(1/789 + 1/724) = 0.051. 95% CI = 1.09 × exp(± 1.96 × 0.051) = 0.99 to 1.21. The crude comparison is compatible with no difference.
  3. SMRs. Exact 95% CI: SMR_A = 0.95 (0.89 to 1.02); SMR_B = 1.23 (1.14 to 1.32). The approximation SMR × exp(± 1.96/√O) gives 0.89 to 1.02 and 1.14 to 1.32 with these large counts. B’s excess mortality is clearly beyond what sampling variation explains; A’s deficit is not.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
sd <- read.csv("data/standardisation_districts.csv")
E_B <- sum(sd$std_rate_per1000 * sd$popB / 1000)
poisson.test(sum(sd$deathsB), E_B)       # SMR for B, exact CI
poisson.test(c(sum(sd$deathsA), sum(sd$deathsB)),
             c(sum(sd$popA), sum(sd$popB)))
    Exact Poisson test
data:  sum(sd$deathsB) time base: E_B
...

Giving poisson.test the observed count and E as the “time base” makes the estimated “event rate” the SMR (1.23) and returns its exact CI (1.14 to 1.32), step 3. With two counts and two populations it returns the crude rate ratio (1.09) with an exact CI of 0.98 to 1.21, slightly different in the second decimal from the log-scale approximation of step 2 (0.99 to 1.21). The p-values are explained in §8.5.

points.html: Does the Poisson model apply? It assumes events occur independently. That is reasonable for all-cause deaths in a district. It is not for cases in an infectious outbreak, where one case causes others; the counts then vary more than Poisson allows and these CIs are too narrow (§13.6 treats this overdispersion).
Relative precision depends on d: SE(ln rate) = 1/√d. 100 events give about ±20%, 400 events about ±10%.

When d is small, the Normal approximation ±1.96√d is poor and can even give a negative lower limit; use exact Poisson limits. There is no fixed cut-off; with a few tens of events or fewer, prefer the exact limits.

blocks.label: Checkpoint 7.6

questions.prompt: Two districts have age-specific death rates of 2 and 20 per 1,000 (District X) and 3 and 24 per 1,000 (District Y) in the under-60 and 60+ groups. Using a standard population of 60,000 under-60 and 40,000 aged 60+, compute both DSRs.
questions.answer: X: expected deaths in the standard = 2 × 60 + 20 × 40 = 120 + 800 = 920; DSR = 920/100,000 × 1,000 = 9.2 per 1,000. Y: 3 × 60 + 24 × 40 = 180 + 960 = 1,140; DSR = 11.4 per 1,000. Y’s standardised mortality is 11.4/9.2 = 1.24 times X’s.

questions.prompt: A PHC catchment records 30 deaths where 20 were expected at state rates. Compute the SMR and its approximate 95% CI. What do you conclude?
questions.answer: SMR = 30/20 = 1.5. SE(ln SMR) = 1/√30 = 0.183. CI = 1.5 × exp(± 1.96 × 0.183) = 1.5 × exp(± 0.358) = 1.05 to 2.15 (exact Poisson: 1.01 to 2.14). Mortality is about 50% above what state rates predict for this age structure; the interval excludes 1, but with only 30 deaths the excess could be anywhere from a few per cent to more than double.

questions.prompt: Why is indirect rather than direct standardisation used for a small PHC catchment?
questions.answer: Direct standardisation needs the catchment’s own age-specific death rates, which rest on very few deaths per age group and are unstable. Indirect standardisation needs only the catchment’s age structure and total deaths, borrowing stable age-specific rates from the standard (state) population.
